newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia interest rate rise seen helping ringgit.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia interest rate rise seen helping ringgit.

text.p: Recovering interest rates are expected to revive the ringgit in the next few days although a rash of positive economic data failed to prevent a sharp fall in the Malaysian unit last week, economists said at the weekend.

They said interbank interest rates were expected to rise after banking institutions forked out two billion ringgit for a seven-year Malaysian government bond issue due on Monday, making the ringgit attractive to foreign investors once again.

It hit a five-month low on Thursday and dipped lower the next day falling below 2.51 on selling triggered by a strong U.S. dollar. The Malaysian unit closed at 2.5075/85 on Friday against 2.5010 a week earlier.

"Foreign funds will return to the ringgit in the week ahead because interest rates are expected to rebound after the payment for the bond," said an analyst with a U.S. bank in Singapore. "Funds will return to the ringgit from Singapore for its yield. I see the ringgit in a 2.5000/5125 range in the near future," he said.
The analysts added that the recent drop in Malaysian interest rates thanks to flush liquidity in the domestic market had made holding the ringgit expensive.
Independent research firm I.D.E.A. has forecast that the rise in short-term interest rates, which started on Friday, would continue in the week ahead.

In addition, economists and foreign exchange dealers said corporate month-end demand for dollars would taper off as would the repatriation of profits by foreign manufacturing firms. Many Japanese firms recently announced their half-year results and various other foreign firms posted third-quarter earnings.
"As a result, there will be less ringgit selling pressure," said a dealer with a Singapore-based European bank.
He said there could also be some delayed reaction to the drop in the growth of broad money supply and an improving external trade balance announced last week.

Bank Negara Malaysia said broad money supply growth, or M3, declined to 21.8 percent year-on-year in August from 25.1 percent in July. However, it was sharply higher than 16.6 percent in the same month last year.
Malaysia's trade deficit for the first seven months of the year was just 1.4 billion ringgit against 6.9 billion in the same period last year.

"The fundamental picture has improved vastly ... but the ringgit is suffering from funds repatriation at the end of the third quarter and a bout of nervousness ahead of the UMNO elections," research firm MMS International said in a market commentary.
UMNO, the United Malays National Organisation, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's political party, is holding its triennial elections in the second week of October.
Some analysts see these party elections as a more important gauge of political stability in the country than the general elections.
Although Mahathir and his deputy, Anwar Ibrahim, have decided not to challenge each other, political analysts have dubbed the elections a fight by proxy through their followers.
Financial analysts said the political factor could keep the ringgit from making sharp gains.
